newsitem.title: UK: Japan investors may cash bonds to ease equity pain.
newsitem.headline: Japan investors may cash bonds to ease equity pain.

text.p: A crumbling Japanese equity market may tempt investors to cash in foreign bond holdings in an effort to re-inflate their shrinking portfolios before the end of the fiscal year, analysts said on Thursday.
But for those Japanese investors who don't need to book profits yet, U.S. Treasuries will continue be the bond market of choice. Japanese government bonds may also provide a haven.
"For some life insurance companies, declines in the Nikkei will obviously mean a reduction in unrealised equity profits," said Peter Wilson, yen strategist at Mitsubishi International.
"They may actually be encouraged to take profits on foreign bond holdings," said Wilson, based in London.

The key Japanese stock market index plunged 3.25 percent on Thursday to 18,073.87, continuing a market rout that has seen the Nikkei 225 index slump 1,287.48 points in the first four trading days of the year.
The market is now at its lowest level in more than a year, amid deepening pessimism over the Japanese economy and the health of the country's banking sector swamped by bad loans.

With Japanese finance officials indicating recently they would prefer a more stable yen, and the end of the 1997 fiscal year approaching on March 31, investors may be enticed to cash in foreign bonds to offset stock losses, Wilson said.
"The evidence we're seeing now is that certain institutions could very well be taking profits with the yen up at 116/117," Wilson said.

The yen was quoted at 116.20 against the dollar at 1310 GMT, continuing a weakening trend since April 1995 that has prompted Japanese investors to borrow yen at low cost, convert currencies and buy foreign debt.
Japanese government bonds may also be a source of cash, particularly for weaker sectors of the banking community whose danger zone on the Nikkei is said to be around 18,500 to 17,500, Wilson said.
"We think they may be selling bonds with high premium, well over par," Wilson said.
But sturdier financial institutions have a danger zone which is much lower and may actually be buyers of JGBs, Wilson added.
Gordon Ross, head of global institutional fixed income at Chase Asset Management, agreed. "That's where I imagine domestic investors will hide. That should underpin the bond market."
Ross noted that an auction for a new 2.7 percent coupon 10-year bond on Thursday went fairly well, despite the equity market turnmoil.
"Four days ago the market would have said that (coupon) would have been too low," he added.
Analysts said, however, that U.S. Treasuries would be the first choice for funds deserting the Japanese stock market.

"There were reports overnight that Japanese investors were buying the dips in the U.S. Treasury market after the sharp fall we saw in the U.S. yesterday," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International Europe in London.

The Japanese were seen to be big investors in U.S. bonds in 1996. They also dabbled in high-yielding European debt as optimism over impending European currency union helped the yields of Italian, Spanish and Swedish bonds converge on Bunds.

But some Japanese investors may shun the high-yielders in 1997 as a decision on which countries take part in European economic and monetary union (EMU) approaches and the rally peters out, analysts said.

"Most Japanese investors go with the view that EMU will go ahead and against that background convergence trades are still favoured, but there are not that many high-yielders left for the Japanese to get into," said Chester.
